correctness.rationale: C1: identify real periodic W¹,∞ derivatives as exactly mean-zero bounded functions. Translation makes convolution at a point the dual norm of the Fejér density modulo constants; L¹ best constants are medians and level sets of nonconstant trigonometric kernels have measure zero, proving attainment. C2: difference-of-squared-sines factorization makes F_(2m+1)-1/(2m+1) sign flip under π translation, hence exact median. C3: joint torus characters k+nℓ establish independent two-angle weak limit; atomless limiting median ensures median convergence. C4: capped identity n(1-Ln)=2E[min(Hn,cn)]-cn avoids nonuniformly integrable unbounded Hn. The triangular integral evaluates to 1/2+2/π² and gives 4/π². Finite checker compares both kernel representations and numerical values; not invoked as a substitute for the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: After eight semantic literature-index searches, comparing accessible mathematical claim statements and examining closely related primary full texts, none of the closest statements implies the sharp periodic Lipschitz seminorm formula, the odd-degree exact medians and the universal 4/π² coefficient. Dobrushin coefficients are in oscillation, Fourier papers concern conjugate approximation or ℓ² smoothing. The earlier sharp Fejér oscillation norm is distinct: it has n=4 factor about 0.883882 versus 0.890451 for the Lipschitz norm. Unindexed literature remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: Older Fourier textbooks or unindexed numerical tables may derive the Fejér median identity without searchable terms.
Some non-open-access historical works were not exhaustively inspected; database nonmatching is not proof of uniqueness.

value.rationale: Classical Fejér means are canonical positive Fourier regularizers; their sharp action on periodic Lipschitz roughness is a natural operator stability invariant independent from pointwise approximation and oscillation contraction. The exact median principle produces actual attaining Lipschitz signals, the odd-degree parity gives a nontrivial explicit optimizer family, and the 4/π² universal first-order deficit quantifies a precise smoothing rate. This is a full asymptotic law for a standard sequence, not a sampled arbitrary finite case or routine normalization check.
